subsystems.name: Waste form
subsystems.role: turns liquid high-level waste into a solid that cannot leak or burn.

subsystems.name: Launch cask
subsystems.role: carries the canister through launch, and survives a launch failure intact.

subsystems.name: Launch vehicle
subsystems.role: lifts the cask out of the atmosphere and out of Earth's gravity well.

subsystems.name: Heliocentric transfer stage
subsystems.role: supplies the large velocity change needed to fall toward the Sun.
parts: high-energy chemical stage or solar-electric thruster

subsystems.name: Trajectory design and navigation
subsystems.role: guarantees the payload hits the Sun and can never return to Earth.

subsystems.name: Tracking and command
subsystems.role: watches every object and can confirm or, if needed, terminate the flight.

subsystems.name: Ground handling
subsystems.role: moves an intensely radioactive cask from storage to the pad without exposing workers.

buildSteps.title: Vitrify the waste
buildSteps.detail: High-level liquid waste is calcined, mixed with glass-forming frit, melted at around 1,100 °C and poured into stainless steel canisters, as is done today at plants such as Sellafield and La Hague.

buildSteps.title: Package for launch
buildSteps.detail: Each canister is sealed inside an overpack engineered to survive a booster explosion, a fall back to Earth and re-entry heating — a far harsher standard than dry storage requires.

buildSteps.title: Prove the containment
buildSteps.detail: Overpacks are drop-tested, fire-tested and impact-tested, and the results are folded into a launch-failure risk assessment.

buildSteps.title: Load at the pad
buildSteps.detail: The cask is transferred in a shielded flask and mated to the upper stage remotely, a slower and more cautious operation than any ordinary payload.

buildSteps.title: Launch and reach orbit
buildSteps.detail: A heavy-lift vehicle places the stack in low Earth orbit while range safety watches for any anomaly.

buildSteps.title: Escape Earth
buildSteps.detail: An upper stage raises the orbit to escape velocity, putting the payload into its own orbit around the Sun.

buildSteps.title: Cancel orbital velocity
buildSteps.detail: This is the hard step. Earth moves around the Sun at about 30 km/s, and to fall inward the spacecraft must shed most of that heliocentric speed — roughly 24 km/s of propulsion, far more than the 12–13 km/s needed to leave the Solar System entirely. A Jupiter gravity assist can supply much of it in exchange for years of extra transit time.

buildSteps.title: Verify the trajectory
buildSteps.detail: Tracking must confirm the perihelion lies inside the Sun and that no future planetary encounter can perturb the object back onto an Earth-crossing path.

buildSteps.title: Dispose of the stage
buildSteps.detail: The final propulsion stage follows the same trajectory, so no spent hardware is left in a stable Earth-orbiting or Earth-crossing state.

prerequisites.why: the waste form itself is already produced routinely; the disposal route is what is missing.

prerequisites.tech: Heavy-lift launch at low cost per kilogram
prerequisites.why: heavy-lift vehicles exist, but reaching the Sun costs several times the energy of reaching low Earth orbit, and the global waste inventory is measured in many thousands of tonnes.

prerequisites.tech: Containment that survives launch failure and re-entry
prerequisites.why: no cask has been qualified to return a fully intact vitrified canister from an exploding booster.

prerequisites.tech: High-energy upper stages and long-life electric propulsion
prerequisites.why: deep-space missions already perform large propulsive manoeuvres over years of cruise.
planetary flybys are standard mission design, and spacecraft such as Ulysses used Jupiter to reach high solar latitudes.

prerequisites.tech: International agreement on launching radioactive waste
prerequisites.why: the Outer Space Treaty, the Liability Convention and the UN principles on nuclear power sources constrain the practice but no framework authorises disposal of this kind.

pathway.milestone: continued vitrification and dry-cask storage, plus deep-space missions that already carry radioactive power sources
pathway.unlocks: a mature waste form and a working safety culture for radioactive payloads.

pathway.milestone: a demonstration flight carrying inert simulant mass on a solar-intercept trajectory
pathway.unlocks: real data on cost, trajectory robustness and public acceptance.

pathway.milestone: a full safety case and an international agreement covering launch cadence, containment standard and trajectory ownership
pathway.unlocks: the legal authority to launch even one cask.

pathway.milestone: a first campaign restricted to separated long-lived actinides rather than bulk spent fuel
pathway.unlocks: a large cut in the radiotoxic lifetime of what remains, if launch costs fall by an order of magnitude.
permanent removal of long-lived isotopes from the biosphere — though deep boreholes and geological repositories are more likely to get there first.
